question.text:
A portfolio manager is assessing two funds: Growth Fund A with a return of 14%, standard deviation of 10%, and beta of 1.2; and Value Fund B with a return of 10%, standard deviation of 8%, and beta of 0.9. The risk-free rate is 5%.
Which fund has a better risk-adjusted return using the Sharpe Ratio?

answer.text: Both have the same Sharpe Ratio.

explanation.text: The Logic: Sharpe Ratio = (Return − Risk-free rate) / Standard Deviation. Growth Fund A = (14% − 5%) / 10% = 0.90. Value Fund B = (10% − 5%) / 8% = 0.625. A higher Sharpe ratio is preferable, so Growth Fund A has the better risk-adjusted return. The Trap: "Both same" tempts those who assume higher return with higher SD produces an identical ratio; "Cannot determine" is wrong because both excess return and standard deviation are supplied. The core misconception is assuming Value B's lower SD alone makes it the winner — the excess-return numerator flips the ranking. Note: Source — NISM-Series-XXI-A workbook (September 2025), pages 148–149, which define Sharpe as excess return over standard deviation and state that a higher Sharpe ratio is preferable.
